title: Human papillomavirus vaccination coverage among adolescent girls and young women living with HIV in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis

analysis.scope_and_question: Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)-attributable cancers disproportionately affect adolescent girls and young women living with HIV (AGYWLHIV) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet HPV vaccination coverage in this subpopulation remains suboptimal.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the pooled prevalence of HPV vaccination coverage among AGYWLHIV in LMICs.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: A total of 8 studies involving 1,059 AGYWLHIV were included in the meta-analysis.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Publication bias and sensitivity analyses were also performed, and statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using the I2 statistic.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Subgroup analyses by age group and vaccine type were conducted, while HPV vaccination delivery platforms were summarised descriptively.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated HPV vaccination coverage among AGYWLHIV in LMICs, finding a pooled coverage of 28.6% with substantial heterogeneity. Subgroup analysis showed higher coverage in younger participants and highlighted the need for integrating HPV vaccination into routine HIV care.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed HPV prevalence and genotype distribution across anogenital sites in Chinese women aged 18–45 years, finding highest prevalence in the vulva and perianal areas, with HPV16 being the most common type. title: Longitudinal viral load trajectories predict cervical lesion risk in women with persistent human papillomavirus infection: A prospective cohort study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the role of longitudinal viral load trajectories in predicting cervical lesion risk among women with persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, addressing the limitation that single viral load measurements may not capture heterogeneous viral dynamics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective cohort study was conducted among 1502 HPV-positive women, with 624 having type-specific persistent infection, followed at approximately 6-month intervals.
analysis.methods: Latent class growth analysis was used to identify viral load trajectories among women with persistent infection, and associations with cervical lesions were assessed using multivariable logistic regression and Firth-penalized regression.
analysis.main_results: Four viral load trajectories were identified: low stable (39.6%), moderate declining (18.9%), moderate increasing (29.8%), and persistently high (11.7%). Any-lesion prevalence was 10.9%, 17.8%, 74.2%, and 90.4%, respectively (p < .001). The persistently high group was strongly associated with cervical lesions, with fully adjusted odds ratios of 124.29 (95% CI, 47.30–326.60) compared to the low-stable group.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study concluded that longitudinal HPV viral load dynamics identified clinically distinct risk phenotypes, with moderate-increasing and persistently high trajectories strongly associated with cervical lesions, improving discrimination beyond baseline measurements.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that longitudinal viral load information can improve the prediction of cervical lesion risk, which could inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the need for external validation before clinical implementation, and the reliance on a prospective cohort with specific inclusion criteria.

analysis.summary_en: This study characterized longitudinal viral load trajectories among women with persistent HPV infection and found that moderate-increasing and persistently high trajectories were strongly associated with cervical lesions, improving prediction beyond baseline measurements.

title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, vaccination, and cervical screening in Britain from 1999 to 2024: findings from the repeated cross-sectional National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal).

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to quantify the impact of HPV vaccination on HPV-16/18 prevalence and uptake of cervical cancer prevention interventions in Britain, addressing the need to inform equitable access to these interventions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used data from three National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) conducted in 1999-2001, 2010-12, and 2022-24, which are nationally representative, cross-sectional population surveys with individual-level data and HPV testing of biosamples.
analysis.methods: The study analysed data from Natsal-2, Natsal-3, and Natsal-4, which included urine biosamples and, in Natsal-4, vaginal swab and urine biosamples, to estimate age-adjusted prevalence ratios for HPV-16/18 infection and assess factors associated with HPV vaccination and cervical screening.
analysis.main_results: The study found that HPV-16/18 prevalence was 86% lower among women aged 18-29 in Natsal-4 compared to Natsal-2, with all HPV-16/18 infections in Natsal-4 occurring in unvaccinated women. Among routine vaccination-eligible women, 23.0% reported being unvaccinated, and 5.3% of women eligible for cervical screening reported never attending screening.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study interpreted that Britain's HPV vaccination programme has significantly reduced HPV-16/18 prevalence, but non-uptake of vaccination and screening remains higher among minority ethnic groups, religious groups, and those born outside the UK, highlighting the need for improved reach of prevention interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that sustained HPV vaccination programmes could achieve WHO cervical cancer elimination targets, but efforts are needed to ensure equitable access and uptake among all population subgroups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the reliance on self-reported data for vaccination and screening uptake, potential biases in the non-probability sample, and the need for further research to understand the long-term impact of the vaccination programme.

analysis.summary_en: This study quantified the impact of HPV vaccination on HPV-16/18 prevalence and cervical cancer prevention uptake in Britain, showing a significant reduction in HPV-16/18 infections but highlighting disparities in vaccination and screening uptake among certain population groups.

analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This narrative review evaluates therapeutic HPV vaccination for recalcitrant warts, nonmelanoma skin cancer and immunocompromised populations.

title: Inactivation of the RB1 and PTPN14 tumor suppressors cooperatively enables the lifespan extension activity of the human papillomavirus E7 oncoprotein

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the cooperative inactivation of RB1 and PTPN14 by high-risk HPV E7 proteins, which are essential for the immortalization of primary human keratinocytes. analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a genetic complementation system with E7 mutants defective for binding to RB1 or PTPN14, expressed in primary human keratinocytes.
analysis.methods: E7 mutants were established and expressed in keratinocytes to assess their ability to extend cell lifespan. Assays were used to measure the inactivation of RB1 and PTPN14, and the effects on keratinocyte differentiation genes.
analysis.main_results: Neither mutant alone could extend keratinocyte lifespan, but when expressed together, they cooperatively extended the lifespan of primary keratinocytes. High-risk HPV E7 reduced RB1 levels and induced E2F-dependent genes, while low-risk HPV6 E7 reduced PTPN14 protein levels and keratinocyte differentiation gene expression.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that inactivation of both RB1 and PTPN14 is required for the lifespan extension activity of high-risk HPV E7, advancing the model of E7 function.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the mechanisms of HPV E7 action and could inform strategies for preventing HPV-associated cancers by targeting these pathways.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the cooperative inactivation of RB1 and PTPN14 by high-risk HPV E7 proteins, showing that both are required for lifespan extension in keratinocytes. The findings advance the understanding of E7 function and could inform cancer prevention strategies.

title: TP53 sequencing and high-risk HPV status in 30 vulvar squamous cell carcinomas with rare combinations of p16 and p53 expression patterns.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Most vulvar squamous cell carcinomas (VSCCs) are classified using p16 and p53 immunohistochemistry into HPV-associated or HPV-independent tumors, but a rare subset demonstrates unusual p16/p53 staining patterns, challenging their classification.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed 30 vulvar squamous cell carcinomas, with the largest subgroup showing p16 positivity and p53 overexpression (n=20). The final case was p16-negative with a mid-epithelial p53 staining pattern, known to be strongly associated with HPV-associated tumors.
analysis.methods: All cases underwent TP53 next-generation sequencing and high-risk HPV (hrHPV) DNA PCR testing to evaluate immunophenotypic and molecular profiles.
analysis.main_results: Of the 20 tumors showing p16 positivity and p53 overexpression, 18 harbored TP53 mutations, while hrHPV DNA was detected in seven, including the two TP53 wild-type tumors. Six tumors showed p16 positivity with absent p53 staining; all harbored TP53 mutations, and two were also hrHPV DNA positive. Three tumors showed p16 positivity confined to the nuclei with p53 overexpression; all harbored TP53 mutations, and one was hrHPV-positive. The final case was p16-negative with a mid-epithelial p53 staining pattern, TP53 wild-type, and hrHPV33-positive.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the rare subset of VSCCs may be better categorized by their immunophenotypic and molecular profiles rather than forced into the current classification, as molecular analysis supported predominantly TP53-driven carcinogenesis with TP53 mutations detected in 93% (27/29) of cases.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the current classification based on p16 and p53 immunohistochemistry may not be sufficient for all VSCCs, and molecular analysis is needed to better understand their biological and clinical significance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its relatively small sample size and the lack of prognostic correlation data, but the evidence is strong as it represents the largest series of such tumors to date and includes detailed molecular analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed 30 vulvar squamous cell carcinomas (VSCCs) with rare combinations of p16 and p53 expression patterns, challenging the current classification system. The largest subgroup showed p16 positivity and p53 overexpression, with TP53 mutations detected in 18 of these cases and hrHPV DNA in seven. Six tumors showed p16 positivity with absent p53 staining, all harboring TP53 mutations, and two were also hrHPV positive. Three tumors showed nuclear p16 positivity with p53 overexpression, all with TP53 mutations, and one was hrHPV positive. The final case was p16-negative with mid-epithelial p53 staining, TP53 wild-type, and hrHPV33-positive. The authors concluded that these rare VSCCs may be better categorized by their immunophenotypic and molecular profiles rather than forced into the existing classification, as molecular analysis supported predominantly TP53-driven carcinogenesis. The study highlights the need for further research to clarify the biological and clinical significance of these tumors.

title: Study on the molecular mechanism of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells inducing epithelial-mesenchymal transition in HPV-associated cervical cancer through activation of miR-129.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the role of miR-129 in HPV-associated cervical cancer, addressing the unclear relationship between bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and miR-129 in tumor progression. HPV-associated cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related death in women worldwide.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved 77 cervical cancer and 30 normal cervical tissue samples, with BMSCs co-cultured with SiHa and HeLa cells to examine miR-129 expression and its effects on cell proliferation, invasion, and EMT marker expression.
analysis.methods: miR-129 expression was measured by qRT-PCR, and associations with clinicopathological features and overall survival were analyzed. Diagnostic value was assessed by ROC curve, and BMSCs were co-cultured with SiHa and HeLa cells to examine miR-129 overexpression or knockdown effects.
analysis.main_results: miR-129 expression was significantly higher in cervical cancer tissues compared to normal controls. High miR-129 expression correlated with tumor size, FIGO stage, and lymph node metastasis, and was associated with shorter overall survival. BMSC co-culture upregulated miR-129 expression, promoting proliferation, colony formation, and invasion, while miR-129 overexpression reduced E-cadherin and increased N-cadherin and MRP1 expression.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the BMSCs/miR-129 axis may contribute to cervical cancer progression, but further in-vivo and mechanistic studies are needed.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study identifies miR-129 as a potential diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for HPV-associated cervical cancer and highlights the role of BMSCs in modulating miR-129 expression and cancer cell phenotypes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of in vitro models and the need for further in-vivo validation. The sample size is relatively small, and the generalizability of the findings may be limited.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the role of miR-129 in HPV-associated cervical cancer, finding that miR-129 is significantly upregulated in cancer tissues and shows potential as a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker. BMSCs upregulate miR-129, promoting cancer cell proliferation and invasion, suggesting a potential therapeutic target but requiring further validation.

analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that HR-HPV infection affected approximately one-third of women screened across seven districts of Western Province, with substantial variation by age and district. title: Presence of Human Papillomavirus and Epstein-Barr Virus in Breast Cancer Biopsies as Potential Risk Factors

analysis.research_question_and_background: Breast cancer represents the leading cause of cancer-related death in the Venezuelan female population. Many risk factors favoring its appearance have been reported; however, human papillomavirus and Epstein-Barr virus have been associated in the past few decades as potential risk factors in the development of this malignancy.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Fresh biopsies were collected from patients with breast cancer and patients with breast benign pathology attending the Hospital Universitario de Caracas for surgery.
analysis.methods: Human papillomavirus detection was made using the INNO-LIPA ® HPV Genotyping Extra commercial kit (Innogenetics), and Epstein-Barr virus genome was detected with Epstein-Barr Virus BMLF1 commercial kit (Maxim Biotech, Inc.).
analysis.main_results: 63.6 and 13.6% of breast cancer cases were positive for human papillomavirus and Epstein-Barr virus DNA, respectively, whereas the benign pathology samples had 4.5% positivity for each one of the viruses; 42.90% of breast cancer samples had mixed infection with low and high oncogenic risk human papillomavirus genotypes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: We can suggest that human papillomavirus and Epstein-Barr virus are important risk factors for breast cancer; however, studies allowing for the role of these viruses in the development of the disease to be elucidated are required.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform future studies on the role of human papillomavirus in breast cancer development and highlight the need for further research to clarify its potential contribution to the disease.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational nature and the lack of detailed statistical analysis, which may affect the strength of the evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the presence of human papillomavirus (HPV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) in breast cancer biopsies to assess their potential role as risk factors. The research is motivated by the fact that breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death in Venezuelan women, and previous associations of HPV and EBV with malignancies have raised questions about their involvement. The study collected fresh biopsies from patients with breast cancer and benign pathology at Hospital Universitario de Caracas. HPV was detected using the INNO-LIPA ® HPV Genotyping Extra commercial kit, while EBV was identified with the Epstein-Barr Virus BMLF1 commercial kit. Results showed that 63.6% of breast cancer cases were positive for HPV DNA, and 13.6% for EBV DNA, compared to 4.5% for each virus in benign samples. Additionally, 42.90% of breast cancer samples had mixed infections with low and high oncogenic risk HPV genotypes. The authors suggest that HPV and EBV may be important risk factors for breast cancer but emphasize the need for further studies to confirm their role. The findings may contribute to understanding the potential involvement of HPV in breast cancer development and highlight the importance of continued research in this area. However, the study's observational design and lack of detailed statistical analysis limit the confidence in its conclusions.

title: Association of non-16/18 high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) genotype multiplicity with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 2+ detection in persistent HPV positivity

analysis.research_question_and_background: To investigate the association between multiple non-16/18 high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) genotype positivity and histologically confirmed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 2+ (CIN2+) among women undergoing colposcopic biopsy because of persistent non-16/18 high-risk HPV positivity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective study evaluated 238 women aged 18–65 years who underwent colposcopic biopsy at a single center after high-risk HPV positivity on at least two consecutive tests performed 12 months or more apart. analysis.methods: HPV multiplicity was defined from the genotype categories reported on the most recent pre-colposcopy test. A post hoc parsimonious logistic regression model included multiplicity and high-risk cytology. The primary outcome was histologically confirmed CIN2+.
analysis.main_results: Of the 238 women, 159 had single-category positivity, and 79 had multiple-category positivity; 25 women had CIN2+. CIN2+ was detected in 14/79 women (17.7%) in the multiple HPV group and 11/159 women (6.9%) in the single HPV group. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that multiplicity of non-16/18 high-risk HPV genotypes may be a marker for increased risk of CIN2+ in women with persistent non-16/18 high-risk HPV positivity, but further research is needed to confirm this association and understand its clinical implications.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the small number of women with CIN2+. The adjustment for high-risk cytology was limited, and the HPV31 subgroup finding was exploratory. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated 238 women with persistent non-16/18 high-risk HPV positivity and found that multiple HPV genotypes were associated with a higher risk of CIN2+, but the association was attenuated after adjustment for high-risk cytology. title: Baseline erythrocyte folate and outcomes of low grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in a prospective cohort

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the association between baseline erythrocyte folate levels and outcomes of low-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN1) in a prospective cohort. The research addressed the knowledge gap regarding the impact of folate on CIN1 progression and provided a rationale for understanding nutritional factors in cervical cancer prevention.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective cohort study was conducted from 2020 to 2024, enrolling 1,503 women with no cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (NC), 564 with CIN1, 218 with CIN2/3, and 2 with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Data were collected through face-to-face interviews and erythrocyte folate levels were measured using chemiluminescence immunoassay.
analysis.methods: Erythrocyte folate levels were measured using a chemiluminescence immunoassay. Cox regression, restricted cubic splines, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used for statistical analyses. The study adjusted for potential confounders such as HR-HPV infection and family history of tumors.
analysis.main_results: Lower baseline erythrocyte folate was associated with adverse CIN1 outcomes, with an adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) of 2.42 (95% CI: 1.62–3.61). No significant nonlinearity was detected at 6 or 12 months, but an L-shaped association was observed at 24 months (P for nonlinearity = 0.005).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that lower baseline erythrocyte folate was associated with adverse CIN1 outcomes after adjustment for confounders. This association was novel and provided insights into the role of folate in CIN1 progression.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that maintaining adequate folate levels may be beneficial in preventing adverse outcomes of CIN1. This could inform surveillance and prevention strategies for cervical cancer.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include event-time assumptions and residual confounding, which limit the interpretation of the results. The evidence strength is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: A prospective cohort study found that lower baseline erythrocyte folate levels were associated with adverse outcomes of CIN1, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.42. This study provides novel insights into the role of folate in CIN1 progression and suggests potential benefits of maintaining adequate folate levels for cervical cancer prevention.

title: Determinants of HPV self-sampling willingness for cervical cancer screening in Urban and Rural Areas of Thailand: An analytical cross-sectional study

analysis.scope_and_question: This study aimed to identify independent factors associated with willingness to use self-HPV testing among women in urban and rural areas of Thailand.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This analytical cross-sectional survey enrolled Thai women aged 25-60 years residing in Saraburi Province, using a structured self-administered questionnaire covering demographic characteristics, HPV knowledge, attitudes, and willingness to use self-HPV testing. Multivariable regression was used to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs).
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: In total, 453 of 527 women (86.0%; 95% CI 82.8%-88.8%) were willing to use self-HPV testing. Knowledge score (PR 1.038 per 10% increase; 95% CI 1.016-1.061) and attitude score (PR 1.092 per 1-point increase; 95% CI 1.022-1.165) were significantly and independently associated with higher willingness, while low household income was significantly associated with lower willingness relative to middle income (PR 0.904; 95% CI 0.830-0.985).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Residential area and screening history were not associated with willingness. The study did not find a statistically significant difference between residential areas, but this finding should not be extrapolated to women without digital access. Knowledge and attitudes were the strongest modifiable determinants identified, and this hypothetical willingness should be distinguished from actual uptake, which remains to be evaluated.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Self-HPV willingness was high in both urban and rural settings among digitally accessible respondents, with no statistically significant difference between residential areas; this finding should not be extrapolated to women without digital access.

analysis.summary_en: This study found that knowledge and attitudes were the strongest modifiable determinants of willingness to use self-HPV testing among Thai women, with high willingness in both urban and rural areas among digitally accessible respondents.

title: Clinical testing source is associated with observed HPV burden in hospital-based cervical HPV genotyping: a retrospective study of 36,362 women

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hospital-based cervical HPV genotyping datasets include women tested through different clinical pathways, so observed HPV burden may vary by source population. We quantified source-specific HPV burden and evaluated cytology-linked context.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a single-center retrospective observational study of 36,362 women with one retained index HPV test per woman. All underwent uniform 23-type cervical HPV genotyping by PCR-reverse dot blot and were classified as health examination attendees or gynecology outpatients by clinical testing source.
analysis.methods: Primary outcomes were any HPV positivity, 12-type carcinogenic HPV positivity, and multiple-genotype infection. Source-group prevalence ratios were adjusted for age group and calendar quarter of testing. Cytology was linked within a prespecified ±3-day window.
analysis.main_results: The cohort included 9,969 health examination attendees and 26,393 gynecology outpatients; cytology was linked for 34,049 women (93.6%). Compared with health examination attendees, gynecology outpatients had higher any HPV positivity (28.7% vs 17.2%; adjusted PR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.54-1.69), 12-type carcinogenic HPV positivity (19.4% vs 10.7%; adjusted PR, 1.75; 95% CI, 1.65-1.86), and multiple-genotype infection (9.2% vs 3.9%; adjusted PR, 2.23; 95% CI, 2.01-2.48).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Clinical testing source was associated with substantial differences in observed HPV burden within a uniform hospital laboratory workflow, highlighting the importance of clinical setting and source population when hospital-based HPV estimates are interpreted.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings caution against interpreting hospital-based HPV estimates without considering the clinical setting and source population, which may influence observed HPV burden and inform more accurate surveillance and diagnosis strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Source-group contrasts were attenuated but remained in the same direction after exclusion of an HPV/STI-related clinical-label subset and after restriction to women with linked cytology. The evidence is moderate due to the retrospective design and potential for residual confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the association between clinical testing source and observed HPV burden in a hospital-based cervical HPV genotyping dataset of 36,362 women. It found that gynecology outpatients had higher rates of any HPV positivity, 12-type carcinogenic HPV positivity, and multiple-genotype infection compared to health examination attendees, even after adjusting for age and testing time. The results highlight the impact of clinical setting on HPV burden estimates. The study was a single-center retrospective observational study using PCR-reverse dot blot for HPV genotyping. Cytology was linked within a ±3-day window. The findings suggest that HPV burden varies by testing source, emphasizing the need to consider clinical context when interpreting hospital-based HPV data. However, the study's retrospective design and potential for residual confounding limit the strength of the evidence, which is assessed as moderate.

analysis.summary_en: Cervical cancer, driven by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. However, current understanding remains uneven, with most studies focusing on isolated mechanisms rather than providing an integrated view of how the HPV-mediated tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) impairs NK cell functions in cervical cancer. This framework provides a unified perspective to guide the development of more effective NK cell–based immunotherapies in cervical cancer.
